Description: ask the patient necessary ice-breaking questions (such as what's the purpose of the visit or any necessary question to make the patient feel comfortable and build connections; these are not related to the symptoms and it is only for ice-breaking) to initiate the interview. the criteria are met when the patient has an elevated or expansive mood
Patient_Story: I have elevated mood. I feel like I am on top of the world. I have been feeling incredibly euphoric, as if I could accomplish anything. I remember staying up late talking with friends, planning an elaborate trip that I impulsively decided we should take, and I even booked the hotel without thinking twice about the cost. However, it all came crashing down when I suddenly felt depressed and withdrawn, barely able to get out of bed for a few days afterward. The stark contrast between those highs and lows has left me feeling a bit confused and concerned about what’s happening to me.

Description: Determine if the patient's elevated or expansive mood is primarily due to the physiological effects of a substance, such as drugs, alcohol, or medications for any medical conditions. The criteria is met when the patient's mood disturbance is directly linked to the substance's effects.
Patient_Story: After that spontaneous road trip, I celebrated with a few drinks at a local bar. I had about five cocktails in a short span, which definitely contributed to the elevated mood I felt afterward. While I was initially excited and carefree, I noticed that the next day, when the effects wore off, I felt a bit low and irritable, which made me wonder if my current happiness was just a result of the alcohol.

Description: Evaluate if the elevated or expansive mood reported by the patient is the primary focus of the clinical picture and is of sufficient severity to require clinical attention. This means the symptoms should be significant enough to cause notable distress or impairment, making them a central concern in the patient's overall condition.
Patient_Story: Lately, I've been experiencing these intense bursts of joy that feel almost electric, like I can conquer anything. Just last week, I had a day where I woke up singing and couldn't contain my excitement; I ended up planning an elaborate surprise party for my best friend, going all out with decorations and invitations. But as much as I love these high moments, I also find myself crashing hard afterward, feeling empty and restless, which leaves me worrying that something deeper might be going on.

Description: Substance/Medication-Induced Bipolar Disorder
Patient_Story: Recently, I started taking a new medication for anxiety, and I’ve noticed some strange changes. After taking it, I felt an overwhelming sense of euphoria that led me to throw a huge party, inviting everyone I knew without a second thought. However, a few days later, I crashed into a deep depression, feeling hopeless and detached, which made me question whether this medication might be the cause of these extreme mood swings.

Description: Substance Intoxication; Substance Withdrawal; Other Adverse Effect of Medication
Patient_Story: I haven't experienced any substance intoxication or withdrawal symptoms, and I don't currently take any medications with adverse effects. In fact, I’ve been quite mindful about my health lately. I only occasionally enjoy a drink socially, like a glass of wine with dinner, but nothing to the extent where I've felt intoxicated or needed to deal with any withdrawal issues.

Description: Determine if the patient's elevated or expansive mood is primarily caused by the physiological effects of a general medical condition, such as physical health issues. This assessment should focus on whether the mood disturbance is directly linked to the underlying medical condition.
Patient_Story: I’ve been feeling really upbeat lately, but I don’t think it’s due to any medical condition. For instance, I had a fantastic week where I aced a challenging work project, and that just filled me with so much joy. I was celebrating with friends and actively engaging in life, which made me feel on top of the world, completely independent of any underlying health issues.

Description: Assess whether the patient shows evidence of decline in one or more cognitive domains, including complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual-motor abilities, or social cognition. This decline should be noticeable and impact the patient's ability to function in these specific areas.
Patient_Story: I haven't noticed any significant decline in my cognitive abilities; in fact, I'm feeling quite sharp these days. Just last week, I managed to organize my schedule for the month, including work tasks, social events, and even a weekend getaway with friends, all without missing a beat. I can still remember details easily and engage in conversations without any issues, which makes me feel confident that I'm functioning well in those areas.

Description: Major or Mild Neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition, with behavioral disturbance
Patient_Story: I haven't experienced any significant cognitive decline or behavioral disturbances due to any medical conditions. In fact, I've been feeling quite mentally sharp, like just last week when I effortlessly worked through some complex problems at work and even helped a colleague who was struggling. My mood has been stable, and I don't feel like there's anything about my mental state that isn't typical for me.

Description: Bipolar and Related Disorder due to another medical condition
Patient_Story: I’ve been managing my asthma for years, but it hasn’t affected my mood or mental state. Just last month, I had a routine check-up where my doctor confirmed that my condition is well-controlled with my daily inhaler, so I haven't noticed any changes in my emotions or behavior that could relate to a bipolar disorder. My day-to-day life feels pretty stable, and I attribute my mood variations to normal life events rather than any underlying medical issues.

Description: the patient has reported clinically significant manic. criteria met for a manic episode (i.e., **at least 1 week of elevated**, expansive or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms sufficiently severe to cause marked impairment). Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: In the past week, I've definitely felt high-spirited and energetic, but I wouldn't say it has reached a level where it has caused any significant impairment in my life. Just yesterday, I had a hectic day at work where I was super productive, staying late to finish projects, but I returned home and easily fell asleep without any racing thoughts or feelings of irritability. While I've enjoyed these bursts of happiness, they usually last only for a day or two, and I haven’t experienced an extended period of elevated mood that affected my day-to-day functioning.

Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.
Patient_Story: I've never had any experiences with delusions or hallucinations. The closest I've come to feeling odd was during a stressful week when I thought I heard someone calling my name in the distance while I was alone at home, but it turned out to be just the wind. It was a little unsettling but nothing more than a passing moment, and I certainly didn’t think it was anything indicative of a mental disorder.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during manic or major depressive episodes.
Patient_Story: I haven't had any psychotic symptoms during periods of mania or depression. For example, even though I've had moments of feeling really high-spirited and joyful, like when I planned that surprise party for my friend, I’ve never experienced hallucinations or delusions during those times or any depressive episodes. My mood shifts seem to be tied to normal life events rather than any manic or major depressive episodes that might bring about psychotic symptoms.

Description: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features
Patient_Story: I’ve never experienced any hallucinations or delusions, even during my high-energy days or when I’ve felt low. For instance, while I did have an intense week last month filled with joy after acing a work presentation, I was completely grounded and rational throughout. My friends often tell me how level-headed I am, and I haven't felt detached from reality or had any strange perceptions at any point in my life.

Description: Schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder
Patient_Story: I’ve never had any experiences that would hint at a schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder. For instance, while I do sometimes feel really happy or low depending on life events, I’ve always been clear-headed and communicative with my friends about how I'm feeling. Just last week, I had a productive meeting at work, and I was able to share my thoughts and ideas without any confusion or strange perceptions—everything felt totally normal and grounded.

Description: Bipolar I disorder
Patient_Story: Lately, I've experienced some periods of elevated mood where I felt incredibly energetic and motivated, but they've always been short-lived. Just last week, after getting great feedback on a project, I felt on top of the world for a couple of days, planning outings with friends and being social. However, I quickly returned to my usual self without any significant shifts in mood or behavior that would suggest a bipolar disorder; everything felt well within the range of my normal ups and downs.

Description: The patient has reported hypomanic and at least one Major Depressive Epsidoe. Criteria met for a hypomanic episode (i.e., at least 4 days of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms not severe enough to cause marked impairment) and has at other times met criteria for a Major Depression Episode.  Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: I’ve had moments of feeling really vibrant and motivated, like just last week when I received praise from my boss after a big presentation. I spent a few days feeling on top of the world, connecting with friends and making plans, but it was all pretty short-lived—I returned to my usual feelings without any significant crash or impairment in my daily life afterward. So, while I've experienced high spirits, I've never had a major depressive episode that matched the criteria described.

Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.
Patient_Story: I've never experienced any delusions or hallucinations throughout my life. There was a time I was feeling particularly stressed, and I thought I heard my phone ringing when it wasn't, but that was just my imagination playing tricks on me. Other than that brief moment, I've always felt grounded in reality and haven't encountered anything that would suggest a mental disorder.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during  major depressive episodes.
Patient_Story: I’ve had some low moments in the past, but they never coincided with any psychotic symptoms. For instance, during a particularly tough week at work, I felt really down and fatigued after a big project fell through, yet I was still fully aware of my surroundings and rational in my thinking. The sadness passed after a few days, and I didn’t experience any hallucinations or delusions during that time, just an understandable reaction to stress.

Description: Bipolar II disorder with psychotic features
Patient_Story: I haven’t experienced any psychotic features like delusions or hallucinations in my life. For instance, even during stressful times, I've always remained grounded—like when I felt overwhelmed after a demanding project at work. While I did have a rough couple of days feeling low, I was still very much aware and understood that my emotions were just a reaction to the situation, not a sign of anything more serious.

Description: Schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder
Patient_Story: I've never had any symptoms that would suggest a schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder. For example, even during a stressful week at work when I felt overwhelmed, I stayed fully connected to reality and never experienced any delusions or hallucinations. My friends often tell me that I have a clear and rational thought process, and I've always managed to articulate my feelings and ideas without confusion.

Description: Bipolar II disorder
Patient_Story: Lately, I've been enjoying some exciting highs, like how I felt over the weekend after scoring a promotion at work. I celebrated with friends, and for a couple of days, I was on cloud nine, making plans and feeling incredibly social. However, I always return to my baseline mood within a short period without experiencing the intense lows that could suggest a bipolar disorder, so everything seems pretty balanced for me.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient explicitly reported at least 2 years of hypomanic symptoms along with periods of depressed mood. Duration should be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: I’ve had moments where I felt really high-spirited, like last summer when I organized a weekend getaway with my friends that was full of laughter and adventure. However, I can't recall experiencing those hypomanic symptoms for a consistent two-year period or having significant depressive episodes afterward. Instead, my mood fluctuations seem to be tied to specific events, and I usually return to my regular self within days.

Description: Cyclothymic
Patient_Story: I've had some joyful moments recently, like last week when I went hiking with friends and felt an incredible sense of happiness while we laughed and shared stories. However, I don’t think I’ve experienced the kind of chronic mood swings or depressive episodes that would make me fit the criteria for cyclothymia. My mood has been stable overall, and these peaks of joy seem to be just a natural part of my life experiences rather than a pattern of mood disorder.

Description: The criteria is met if elevated or euphoric mood confined to periods of gambling
Patient_Story: I've never experienced an elevated or euphoric mood specifically linked to gambling. In fact, I rarely gamble at all; the last time I placed a bet was at a friend's wedding just for fun, where I put down a few dollars on a game, but it didn't lead to any heightened feelings afterward. My mood has generally been stable, influenced more by everyday events rather than any gambling-related excitement.

Description: The criteria are met if the persistent and problematic gambling behaviour leads to clinically significant impairment or distress. This means the symptoms should be significant enough to cause notable distress or impairment, making them a central concern in the patient's overall condition.
Patient_Story: I’ve never had the urge to gamble excessively or felt that it was a central concern in my life. I remember the last time I was at a casino with friends, I placed a few small bets on the blackjack table just for the fun of it, but I quickly lost interest and moved on to enjoy the live music. It was a casual experience without any lingering need or distress related to gambling, so I don’t think it’s ever been a problem for me.

Description: Gambling Disorder
Patient_Story: I've never experienced any compulsive gambling behavior or felt the thrill of betting as a central part of my life. The last time I visited a casino was on a friend's birthday, where I casually played a few rounds of poker with some friends, but I didn't invest much money or time into it. After a couple of games, I lost interest and joined everyone else for dinner, so it never felt significant to me.

Description: Normal Gambling Behavior
Patient_Story: I've never really been drawn to gambling in any serious way. I remember going to a friend's wedding where we had a little fun playing games, and I placed a few bets, but it was all lighthearted—just a few dollars for entertainment. Afterward, I completely forgot about it and spent the rest of the evening dancing and enjoying the celebration rather than thinking about the gambling at all.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient exhibits a maladaptive response to a psychosocial stressor, meaning their response is disproportionate or ineffective, leading to significant distress or impairment in functioning.
Patient_Story: Recently, I went through a tough project at work that felt overwhelming at times, but I managed to cope fairly well. After receiving some critical feedback, I took a couple of days to reflect and regroup rather than spiraling into distress; I reached out to friends for support and created a plan to tackle my responsibilities. This proactive approach helped me regain my balance without any significant impairment in my daily functioning.

Description: Other specified bipolar and related disorder; unspecified bipolar and related disorder
Patient_Story: I've never experienced the kind of mood fluctuations or episodes that would suggest a bipolar disorder. For instance, while I have had some days where I felt particularly happy, like when I received compliments on my work presentation and wanted to celebrate with friends, those feelings were short-lived and didn’t lead to any significant changes in my behavior or mood that would indicate something more serious. My emotions seem to be directly tied to specific events, and I usually find myself back to normal quite quickly.

Description: "Normal" elevated or euphoric mood
Patient_Story: I wouldn't say I've experienced a sustained elevated or euphoric mood. While I do enjoy moments of happiness, like when I celebrated a friend's birthday last week, those feelings tend to be brief and closely tied to specific events. After the party, I returned to my usual routine without any significant mood changes, so I feel that my emotional state remains quite stable overall.

Description: Healthy
Patient_Story: I've been feeling pretty stable lately, with no significant mood changes. Just last week, I finished a project at work and felt satisfied but not overly euphoric. I celebrated by going out for dinner with friends, but it was a casual outing, and afterward, I went home and relaxed, feeling completely normal.
